title: Aretius and Polanus: mercy in God and gifts of the Spirit
source_text: III. Similiter Aretius in locis communibus loco vigesimo quinto docet sacras literas, quum de gratia loquuntur, primo hac voce intelligere gratuitam Dei misericordiam qua se manifestat in hominis reconciliatione & justificatione. Deinde per gratiam significare quoque dona Spiritus sancti, quae dona ibidem agnoscit recte dici posse gratiam infusam. Et eodem recidit distinctio Polani. Gratia Dei, inquit, ὁμωνύμως dicitur, Est enim vel in Deo residens, vel a Deo data. In Syntagmate Theologiae Christianae parte 1. lib. 2. cap. 21.
pass_a_gloss: III. Similarly Aretius in the commonplaces in the twenty-fifth place teaches that the sacred writings, when they speak of grace, first understand by this word the free mercy of God by which he manifests himself in the reconciliation and justification of man. Then by grace they signify also the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which gifts he there acknowledges can rightly be called infused grace. And to the same falls back the distinction of Polanus. The grace of God, he says, is said homonymously, For it is either residing in God, or given by God. In the Syntagma of Christian Theology part 1. book 2. chap. 21.
pass_b_english: Thesis III. Likewise Aretius, in locus 25 of his commonplaces, teaches that when scripture speaks of grace, it means by the word first God's free mercy, by which he shows himself in reconciling and justifying a person.

Next, it uses grace for the gifts of the Holy Spirit as well, and he grants there that these gifts may rightly be called infused grace. Polanus's distinction comes to the same thing. The grace of God, he says, is spoken of homonymously, that is, in two senses: it is either grace that resides in God or grace given by God (Syntagma of Christian Theology, part 1, book 2, chapter 21).
